name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
summary: A Democrat who answered the Great Depression with the New Deal: banking and securities regulation, work relief, Social Security, labor-rights and wage-and-hours laws, public power through the TVA, and higher taxes on large incomes, always defending private enterprise and constitutional democracy. He moved the United States from neutrality toward aid to the Allies, led it in World War II, ordered the removal of Japanese Americans from the West Coast, and made a postwar United Nations a central goal.

universal-healthcare.rationale: In 1944 he listed a right to adequate medical care among the economic rights and in 1941 urged wider opportunities for medical care, but he left health insurance out of the 1935 Social Security program and never proposed a universal state system.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: He backed legal minimum wages (he signed the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, which set a federal minimum) and in 1944 called for the right to earn enough for adequate food, clothing and recreation; he never named a figure for a substantial rise.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: He held that unregulated markets had failed and that private enterprise needed government assistance and safeguards, while still treating private enterprise as necessary to democracy.

public-ownership.rationale: He created the TVA and defended public power as a yardstick and the right of communities to own utilities, but he opposed general government entry into business and relied on regulation for rail and other utilities.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: He signed the Revenue Act of 1935, which raised taxes on the highest earners (top rate 79 percent), and in 1941 and 1944 insisted on taxing in accordance with ability to pay and on taxing all unreasonable war profits.

unions-good.rationale: He signed the Wagner Act guaranteeing collective bargaining through unions of workers' own choice and said workers needed effective power to bargain collectively, naming those who refuse it as the source of class dissension.

property-fundamental.rationale: He called private economic power a public trust and said all property rights must yield to the safety of people's savings, so property could be restricted when needed to protect others.

regulate-corporations.rationale: He demanded stricter supervision of banking, securities and utilities, signed the securities laws and the SEC, and declared that government by organized money was as dangerous as government by mob.

cut-welfare.rationale: He rejected ending relief as 'purging the rolls by starvation' and signed Social Security, while preferring work relief to the dole; he did not accept that aid should be cut.

notes: Answers rest on his own speeches and messages (1932-1945) and on the record of laws and orders he signed. Where views changed, the later position is used: his 1932 pledge to balance the budget gave way to deficit-financed relief; peacetime neutrality gave way to aid to the Allies and a call for a world organization. His 1937 letter held that collective bargaining cannot be transplanted into the public service and that strikes of federal employees are intolerable; his support for unions applies to private-sector workers. One answer is inferred (marked 'Inferred:') and is low confidence. No position was recorded for many cultural, religious and gender statements; none were guessed.
